beats.lead: The tool almost every business course teaches
beats.text: SWOT analysis is usually credited to Harvard Business School's planning course, or to Albert Humphrey inventing it alone at Stanford.
beats.note: A 2023 peer-reviewed history in the journal Long Range Planning found that neither claim holds up.

beats.name: Robert F. Stewart
beats.role: Led the long-range planning group at the Stanford Research Institute where the framework was actually built, and first called it SOFT, not SWOT.

beats.text: SOFT stood for Satisfactory, Opportunity, Fault, Threat: the present and future of an organisation, sorted into what was working and what was not.
beats.note: Albert Humphrey worked on the same SRI team. He relabelled it SWOT, for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats, in a paper he published in 1974.

beats.text: The Harvard Business School origin story does not hold up either.
beats.note: William Guth, the last surviving member of Harvard's 1960s policy faculty, said in 2017 he was confident no one on that faculty created the framework.

beats.text: A tool built to help you check your assumptions had one about its own history.

beats.line: SWOT was not Harvard's, and it was not only Humphrey's.
